                                                                                     Lipschitz widths
                                                                       Guergana Petrova, Przemyslaw Wojtaszczyk ∗

                                                                                       November 3, 2021




arXiv:2111.01341v1 [math.NA] 2 Nov 2021
                                                                   To Ron DeVore, with the utmost respect and admiration

                                                                                             Abstract
                                                      This paper introduces a measure, called Lipschitz widths, of the optimal performance possible
                                                  of certain nonlinear methods of approximation. It discusses their relation to entropy numbers
                                                  and other well known widths such as the Kolmogorov and the stable manifold widths. It also
                                                  shows that the Lipschitz widths provide a theoretical benchmark for the approximation quality
                                                  achieved via deep neural networks.
                                                  AMS subject classification: 41A46, 41A65, 82C32
                                                  Key words: widths, entropy numbers, neural networks


                                          1       Introduction
                                          Nonlinear methods of approximation provide reliable and eﬃcient ways of investigating the under-
                                          lying phenomena in many application areas. Despite of their extensive usage however, there is still
                                          a lack of comprehensive understanding of the intrinsic limitations of these nonlinear methods, even
                                          on a purely theoretical level. Several mathematical concepts, called widths, have been established
                                          to access numerous aspects of the quality of linear and nonlinear approximations. As such, we men-
                                          tion the classical by now Kolmogorov, linear, manifold, Gelfand widths, which give a theoretical
                                          benchmark on what is the best possible performance of particular methods of approximation, see
                                          [8], where a summary of diﬀerent nonlinear widths and their relations to one another is discussed.
                                               Recently, Deep Neural Networks (DNN) have been used extensively as a method of choice for
                                          variety of machine learning problems and as a computational platform in many other areas. Despite
                                          of their empirical successes, the explanation of the reasons behind their stellar performance is still
                                          in its infancy. On mathematical level, DNN can be viewed as a method of nonlinear approximation
                                          of an underlying function f , where the approximant Φ(y) ≈ f is a continuous function, generated
                                          by a DNN with parameters y. It can be shown that the mapping which to every choice of param-
                                          eters y of the DNN assigns Φ(y) is in fact a Lipschitz mapping. Thus, DNN approximation is a
                                          particular case of a nonlinear approximation of a function f , or a compact class K, by the images of
                                          Lipschitz mappings. Then, the question of DNN optimal performance is intimately related to the
                                          quantiﬁcation of the optimal performance of such nonlinear methods and to the introduction and
                                          study of corresponding ways to measure it. A width, called stable manifold width, was presented
                                              G.P. was supported by the NSF Grant DMS 2134077, Tripods Grant CCF-1934904, and ONR Contract N00014-
                                              ∗

                                          20-1-278. P. W. was supported by National Science Centre, Polish grant UMO-2016/21/B/ST1/00241.


                                                                                                 1
in [5], with the sole purpose to determine the optimal performance of such nonlinear methods in
the context of numerical computation, where the stability plays an essential role. In this paper, we
take a slightly diﬀerent point of view and introduce the concept of Lipschitz widths, where we are
not so concerned about the numerical stability of the method, but rather about the best possible
performance of these nonlinear methods of approximation.
    Our setting is a Banach space X equipped with a norm k · kX , where we wish to approximate
the elements f of a compact subset K ⊂ X of X with error measured in this norm. For every
ﬁxed n ∈ N and every γ ≥ 0, the approximants to K will come from the images Φ(y) ∈ X of
γ-Lipschitz maps Φ : (BYk , k · kYk ) → X, where k ≤ n, and BYk is the unit ball in Rk with respect
to some norm k · kYk in Rk . The quality of this approximation is a critical element in the design and
analysis of various numerical methods, among which are DNNs. Note that any numerical method
based on Lipschitz mappings will have performance no better than the optimal performance of this
approximation method. On the other hand, it may not be easy to actually design a numerical
method for a particular application that achieves this optimal performance.
    In our analysis, we examine model classes K ⊂ X, i.e., compact subsets K of X, that summarize
what we know about the target function f . Classical model classes K are ﬁnite balls in smoothness
spaces like the Lipschitz, Sobolev, or Besov spaces. The Lipschitz widths dγn (K)X then quantify the
best possible performance of the above approximation methods on a given model class K.
    The paper is organized as follows. Some of the basic properties of Lipschitz widths are discussed
in §2 and §3, where it is shown that for a ﬁxed n ∈ N, dγn (K)X is a continuous function of γ ≥ 0,
see Theorem 2.5. We also prove the statements
                              lim dγ (K)X = 0,       and    lim dγ (K)X = 0,
                             n→∞ n                         γ→∞ n

each of which characterizes the set K as a totally bounded set, see Lemma 2.6 and Lemma 2.9.
   The relation between Lipschitz widths and entropy numbers εn (K)X is investigated in §4, The-
orem 4.2, where among other things, we show that for any compact subset K ⊂ X of a Banach
space X we have
                              dn2 rad(K) (K)X ≤ εn (K)X , n = 1, 2, . . . .
Examples are given to show that this inequality is almost optimal. We also discuss in this sec-
tion estimates from below and above for the Lipschitz width dγn (K)X , provided bounds for the
entropy numbers εn (K)X are available, see Corollary 4.8. Some of our estimates are optimal, as
demonstrated in Theorem 4.10, where we show that the Lipschitz widths could be smaller than the
entropy numbers for certain compact classes K.
    Since the Lipschitz width is a new concept of width, we compare it with some of the well known
classical widths. We show that for appropriate values of the parameter γ, Lipschitz widths are
smaller than the Kolmogorov widths, see §5, Theorem 5.1. They are also smaller than the stable
manifold widths, see §6, Theorem 6.1. However, as demonstrated by the provided Examples, in
both cases, their actual behavior may be very diﬀerent.
    At last, in §7, we discuss the Lipschitz widths dγnn (K)X with γn = C ′ nδ λn and show that they
provide a theoretical benchmark for the performance of certain DNN approximation, see Theorem
7.1. The analysis of these widths is performed in Theorem 7.3 and Corollary 7.4, where it is
demonstrated that there is indeed a gain in the performance of the Lipschitz width dγnn (K)X when
compared to the entropy numbers εn (K)X in the following sense
                                         [log2 n]β                       [log2 n]β
                        if   εn (K)X ≍                ⇒    dnγn (K)X ≍             .
                                            nα                              n2α

                                                      2
This estimate, when applied in the case of K being the unit ball of certain Besov spaces, extends
the results from [6] to the case when error is measured in Lp , p 6= ∞.


2      Definition and basic properties
We are mainly interested in compact sets, however we deﬁne the basic concepts for bounded sets.
We consider a bounded subset K ⊂ X of a Banach space (X, k · kX ) with norm k · kX and denote
by (Rn , k.kYn ), n ≥ 1 the n-dimensional Banach space with a ﬁxed norm k · kYn . For γ ≥ 0, we
deﬁne the fixed Lipschitz width

                              dγ (K, Yn )X := inf sup inf kf − Φn (y)kX ,                     (2.1)
                                               Φn f ∈K y∈BYn


where the inﬁmum is taken over all Lipschitz mappings

                       Φn : (BYn , k · kYn ) → X,      BYn := {y ∈ Rn : kykYn ≤ 1},

that satisfy the Lipschitz condition

                                               kΦn (y) − Φn (y ′ )kX
                                       sup                           ≤ γ,                     (2.2)
                                    y,y ′ ∈BYn     ky − y ′ kYn

with constant γ. Next, we deﬁne the Lipschitz width

                                    dγn (K)X := inf inf dγ (K, Yk )X ,                        (2.3)
                                                    k≤n k·kYk


where the inﬁmum is taken over all norms k · kYk in Rk and all k ≤ n. Clearly, we have that for
every norm k · kYn on Rn ,
                               dγn (K)X ≤ dγ (K, Yn )X , n ≥ 1.                           (2.4)
  Before going further, let us recall the deﬁnition of a diameter and radius of a bounded set
M ⊂ X,
              diam(M) := sup kf − gkX ≤ 2 inf sup kf − gkX =: 2 rad(M).
                                f,g∈M                       g∈X f ∈M

From (2.2) we see that a 0-Lipschitz function is simply the constant function. Thus, for any Yn we
get
                                 rad K = d0n (K, Yn )X = d0n (K)X .                           (2.5)
    We next list some elementary properties of the Lipschitz widths dγn (K)X that we gather in the
following lemma.

Lemma 2.1. For any bounded subset K ⊂ X of a Banach space X, any n ∈ N, and any γ > 0, we
have

    (i) The Lipschitz width dγn (K)X is given by

                                          dγn (K)X = inf dγ (K, Yn )X .                       (2.6)
                                                         k·kYn




                                                        3
 (ii) We can restrict the infimum in (2.6) only to normed spaces (Rn , k.kYn ) with the additional
      property that the norm k · kYn satisfyies the condition
                                              n
                                              X
             kykℓn∞ := max |yj | ≤ kykYn ≤          |yj | =: kykℓn1 ,   y = (y1 , y2 , . . . , yn ) ∈ Rn .    (2.7)
                            j
                                              j=1


(iii) The space (Rn , k · kYn ) in (2.1) and (2.6) can be replaced by any normed space (Xn , k · kXn )
      of dimension n, that is

         dγn (K)X = inf dγ (K, Xn )X ,     where      dγ (K, Xn )X = inf sup inf kf − Φn (x)kX ,              (2.8)
                    k·kXn                                                Φn f ∈K x∈BXn


     with BXn := {x ∈ Xn : kxkXn ≤ 1}.

(iv) dγn (K)X is a monotone decreasing function of γ and n. More precisely,

        • If γ1 ≤ γ2 then dγn2 (K)X ≤ dγn1 (K)X ;
        • If n1 ≤ n2 then dγn2 (K)X ≤ dγn1 (K)X .

 (v) For every fixed n ∈ N and γ ≥ 0, we have dγn (K)X ≤ rad(K) < ∞.

(vi) For every fixed n ∈ N and γ ≥ 0, we have dγn (K)X = dγn (K̄)X where K̄ denotes the closure of
     K.

Proof: Since
                                       dγn (K)X ≤ inf dγ (K, Yn )X ,
                                                    k·kYn

to show (i), it suﬃces to show that for every norm k · kYk with 1 ≤ k < n, there exists a norm k · kYn
on Rn such that
                                     dγ (K, Yn )X ≤ dγ (K, Yk )X .                              (2.9)
Indeed, let us ﬁx a γ-Lipschitz map Φk : (BYk , k · kYk ) → X which achieves dγ (K, Yk )X (if such map
does not exist, we can use limiting arguments). We then deﬁne the norm k · kYn as

                                    k(y, y ′ )kYn := kykYk + ky ′ kRn−k ,

where k.kRn−k is any norm in Rn−k , and a mapping Φn : (BYn , k · kYn ) → X as

                                          Φn ((y, y ′ )) := Φk (y).

Clearly, Φn is a γ-Lipschitz mapping since

      kΦn ((y, y ′ )) − Φ((z, z ′ ))kX = kΦk (y) − Φk (z)kX ≤ γky − zkYk ≤ γk(y, y ′ ) − (z, z ′ )kYn ,

and thus (2.9) holds.
Next, we use (i) to prove (ii). Let (Rn , k · kYn ) be any normed space. It follows from the Auerbach
lemma (see e.g. [4, p.43] or [14, II.E.11]), that we can ﬁnd vectors (v̄j )nj=1 ⊂ Rn and linear

In addition, Φ̃n (BYn ) = Φn (BYn ), and therefore (ii) follows from (i).
    To prove (iii), we ﬁx a basis {φ1 , . . . , φn } ∈ Xn , the mapping κ : Xn → Rn given by
                                                                                     n

is isometry between (Xn , k · kXn ) and (Rn , k · kYn ), where kxkYn := kgkXn . Thus, each norm k · kYn
on Rn induces a norm k · kXn on Xn and vice versa. Moreover, the mappings Φn ◦ κ : BXn → X
and Φn : BYn → X have the same Lipschitz constants, which shows the equivalence of the two
deﬁnitions (2.6) and (2.8).
     Next, (iv) and (vi) follow directly from the deﬁnition, and (v) follows from (2.5) and (iv). ✷

                                                                     5
2.1   Packing, covering and entropy numbers
Before going further, we recall in this section the well known concepts of packing, covering, and
entropy numbers for compact sets M, which we will use in our study of Lipschitz widths. The
reader may ﬁnd a more detailed exposition of those concepts in many books, see, for example,
[4, 13, 12].
    Minimal ε-covering number Nε (M) of a compact set M ⊂ X:
A collection {g1 , . . . , gm } ⊂ X of elements of X is called an ε-covering of M if
                       m
                       [
                 M⊂          B(gj , ε),    where B(gj , ε) := {f ∈ X : kf − gj kX ≤ ε}.
                       j=1

An ε-covering of M whose cardinality is minimal is called minimal ε-covering of M. We denote
by Nε (M) the cardinality of the minimal ε-covering of M.
    Minimal inner ε-covering number Ñε (M) of a compact set M ⊂ X:
It is deﬁned exactly as Nε (M) but we additionally require that the centers {g1 , . . . , gm } of the
covering are elements from M.
    Entropy numbers εn (M)X of a compact set M ⊂ X:
For every ﬁxed n ≥ 0, the entropy number εn (M)X is the inﬁmum of all ε > 0 for which 2n balls
with centers from X and radius ε cover M. If we put the additional restriction that the centers of
these balls are from M, then we deﬁne the so called inner entropy number ε̃n (M)X . Formally, we
write
                                             [2n
                 εn (M)X = inf{ε > 0 : M ⊂       B(gj , ε), gj ∈ X, j = 1, . . . , 2n },
                                                      j=1

                                                      2n
                                                      [
                ε̃n (M)X = inf{ε > 0 : M ⊂                  B(hj , ε), hj ∈ M, j = 1, . . . , 2n }.
                                                      j=1

   Maximal ε-packing number P̃ε (M) of a compact set M ⊂ X:
A collection {f1 , . . . , fℓ } ⊂ M of elements from M is called an ε-packing of M if

                                              min kfi − fj kX > ε.
                                               i6=j


An ε-packing of M whose size is maximal is called maximal ε-packing of M. We denote by P̃ε (M)
the cardinality of the maximal ε-packing of M.
   We have the following inequalities for every ε > 0 and every compact set M

                                          P̃ε (M) ≥ Ñε (M) ≥ P̃2ε (M),                               (2.14)

                                     εn (M)X ≤ ε̃n (M)X ≤ 2εn (M)X .                                  (2.15)

Remark 2.2. Let us recall the classical relations between those concepts and compactness. We call
the set M totally bounded if for every ε > 0 we have Nε (M) < ∞. This is equivalent to the fact
that limn→∞ εn (M)X = 0. Each compact set is totally bounded. Actually a subset M of a Banach
space is compact if and only if it is totally bounded and closed. The interested reader will find a
detailed study on the topic in many books on functional analysis or metric topology.


                                                           6
Remark 2.3. In what follows later, we will use the fact that the Lipschitz widths and the entropy
numbers are invariant with respect to translation, that is, for any n ∈ N, γ ≥ 0, and any f ∈ X we
have
                        dγn (K)X = dγn (K − f )X , εn (K)X = εn (K − f )X .

2.2   Dependence of dγn (K)X on γ
We start this section by proving the fact that the Lipschitz width dγn (K)X is a continuous function
of γ. To do that, we ﬁrst prove the following lemma.

Lemma 2.4. For every n ≥ 1, every γ > 0, and every norm k · kYn in Rn , the fixed Lipschitz width
dγ (K, Yn )X satisfies the inequality

                                    rad(K) − γ ≤ dγ (K, Yn )X ≤ rad(K).                       (2.16)

Proof: If we ﬁx g ∈ X and take Φ(y) = g for every y ∈ BYn , we have that Φ is γ-Lipschitz for
every γ > 0 and thus
                               dγ (K, Yn )X ≤ sup kf − gkX ,
                                                      f ∈K

which gives dγ (K, Y   n )X ≤ rad(K).
                                  To show the left hand-side inequality in (2.16), we notice that
for any γ-Lipschitz map Φ, every f ∈ K and y ∈ BYn we have

               kf − Φ(y)kX ≥ kf − Φ(0)kX − kΦ(0) − Φ(y)kX ≥ kf − Φ(0)kX − γ,

since kΦ(0) − Φ(y)kX ≤ γkykYn ≤ γ. Therefore we obtain the inequality

                              sup inf kf − Φ(y)k ≥ sup kf − Φ(0)k − γ,
                              f ∈K y∈BYn                   f ∈K

which gives
                                   dγ (K, Yn )X ≥ inf sup kf − Φ(0)kX − γ.                    (2.17)
                                                  Φ f ∈K

Note now that for every Φ,

                            sup kf − Φ(0)kX ≥ inf sup kf − gkX = rad(K),
                            f ∈K                  g∈X f ∈K


and thus it follows from (2.17) that

                                         dγ (K, Yn )X ≥ rad(K) − γ,

and the proof is completed.                                                                       ✷

Theorem 2.5. For every compact subset K ⊂ X of a Banach space X and any n ∈ N, the Lipschitz
width dγn (K)X is a continuous function of γ ≥ 0.

Proof: We ﬁrst show the continuity of the Lipschitz width at γ = 0. It follows from Lemma 2.4
and Lemma 2.1, (i) that
                              rad(K) − γ ≤ dγn (K)X ≤ rad(K).


                                                     7
We let γ → 0 and obtain
                                 lim dγn (K)X = rad(K) = d0n (K)X ,
                                 γ→0

which proves the continuity at γ = 0, see (2.5).
   To show that the Lipschitz width is continuous for γ > 0, we ﬁx n ∈ N and denote by

                                            h(γ) := dγn (K)X .

According to Lemma 2.1, (v), h(γ) < ∞ for every γ > 0. Let us assume that h is not a continuous
function. Then, there exist γ0 > 0, δ > 0, and a sequence of positive numbers εk → 0, such that

                            h(γ0 + εk ) + δ ≤ h(γ0 − εk ),       for every k.               (2.18)

We ﬁx ε := εk < γ0 . From the deﬁnition of Lipschitz widths, there exists a (γ0 + ε)-Lipschitz map
Φn : (BYn , k · kYn ) → X such that

                       h(γ0 + ε) ≤ sup inf kf − Φn (y)kX ≤ h(γ0 + ε) + ε.                   (2.19)
                                      f ∈K y∈BYn

Now we deﬁne the mapping
                                                        γ0 − ε
                       Φ̃n := ξΦn ,     where ξ :=               and 0 < ξ < 1.
                                                        γ0 + ε

Clearly, Φ̃n is a (γ0 − ε)-Lipschitz mapping, and therefore

         h(γ0 − ε) ≤ sup inf kf − Φ̃n (y)kX = sup inf kξ(f − Φn (y)) + (1 − ξ)f kX
                        f ∈K y∈BYn                      f ∈K y∈BYn
                    ≤ sup inf (ξkf − Φ(y)kX + (1 − ξ)kf kX )
                        f ∈K y∈BYn
                    ≤ ξ sup inf kf − Φn (y)kX + (1 − ξ) sup kf kX
                          f ∈K y∈BYn                              f ∈K
                    ≤ ξ(h(γ0 + ε) + ε) + (1 − ξ)C,

where we have used (2.19) and the fact that supf ∈K kf kX = C < ∞ (since K is compact). The
latter inequality and (2.18) give

                     h(γ0 + ε) + δ ≤ h(γ0 − ε) ≤ ξ(h(γ0 + ε) + ε) + (1 − ξ)C

which is a contradiction for a suﬃciently small ε = εk since ξ → 1 as εk → 0.                 ✷
    We ﬁnish the investigation of the behavior of the Lipschitz width with respect to γ with the
following lemma.
Lemma 2.6. For any K ⊂ X, the set K is totally bounded iff for every n ≥ 1

                                            lim dγ (K)X = 0.
                                           γ→∞ n

Proof: Assume that K is totally bounded. From the monotonicity of the Lipschitz width with
respect to n, see Lemma 2.1, (iii), it suﬃces to consider only the case n = 1. For δ > 0, we ﬁx a
                            Nδ (K)

    We now ﬁx n ≥ 1 and show that limγ→∞ dγn (K)X = 0 implies that K is totally bounded. We

δ0 > 0 and an inﬁnite δ0 -packing set that we will denote (hj )∞   j=1 .

    Let us ﬁx a norm k · kYn on R and consider any γ-Lipschitz map Φ : (BYn , k · kYn ) → X. We
then take ǫ < δ0 /3γ and denote by {yj }N   j=1 ⊂ BYn a ﬁnite ǫ-covering of BYn .
    Note that at most one hi can belong to any of the sets B(Φ(yj ), δ0 /2). Indeed, if we assume

                        kΦ(y) − Φ(yj ∗ )kX ≤ γky − yj ∗ kYn ≤ γε < δ0 /3.                         (2.21)

              khs − Φ(y)kX ≥ khs − Φ(yj ∗ )kX − kΦ(y) − Φ(yj ∗ )kX ≥ δ0 /2 − δ0 /3 = δ0 /6,
which gives

and therefore
                                              dγn (K)X ≥ δ0 /6.                                  (2.22)
Notice that the choice of γ is arbitrary, so we have the above inequality for every γ, and the proof
is completed.                                                                                     ✷

                                                       9
Remark 2.7. Note that all statements in this paper are valid for sets K whose closures are compact
rather than sets K that are compact. Therefore, since we work in Banach spaces, all statements are
valid for K being only a totally bounded set rather than a compact set.

Remark 2.8. It follows from the proof of Lemma 2.6, see (2.22), that if K is not totally bounded
then there exists δ > 0 such that
                                       inf dγn (K)X ≥ δ.
                                         γ>0,n>0


2.3   Dependence of the Lipschitz width dγn (K)X on n.
In this section we discuss the behavior of the Lipschitz width with respect to n. The following
Lemma holds.

Lemma 2.9. Let K ⊂ X be a subset of a Banach space X. If there exists γ > 0 such that
limn→∞ dγn (K)X = 0, then K is totally bounded (i.e. its closure is compact).

Proof: To prove the lemma, we ﬁx η > 0 and show that K is contained in the union of a ﬁnite
collection of balls with radius η. Since limn→∞ dγn (K)X = 0, we can ﬁnd an integer n0 such that

                                            dγn0 (K)X < η/2,

and therefore there exists a norm k · kYn0 in Rn0 and a γ-Lipschitz map Φ : (BYn0 , k · kYn0 ) → X
such that
                                  sup inf kf − Φ(y)k < η/2.
                                    f ∈K y∈BYn0

More precisely, for every f ∈ K, we can ﬁnd y ∈ BYn0 such that

                                         kf − Φ(y)kX < η/2.                                       (2.23)

Let {yj }N
         j=1 ⊂ BYn0 be an η/(2γ)-covering for the compact set BYn0 , that is

                                               N
                                               [
                                      BYn0 ⊂         B(yj , η/(2γ)),
                                               n=1

and therefore for every y ∈ BYn0 we can ﬁnd yj , j ∈ {1, 2, . . . , N }, such that ky − yj kYn0 ≤ η/(2γ).
Thus we have
                             kΦ(y) − Φ(yj )kX ≤ γky − yj kYn0 ≤ η/2,
and
                                                  N
                                                  [
                                    Φ(BYn0 ) ⊂          B(Φ(yj ), η/2).
                                                  n=1
                                                     S
From the latter result and (2.23) it follows that K ⊂ N
                                                      n=1 B(φ(yj ), η), and the proof is completed.
✷
   The converse statement of Lemma 2.9 is also true, see Corollary 4.3 and Corollary 5.3.

3      Further properties of Lipschitz widths
3.1     Properties of Lipschitz mappings
Before focusing our attention on the Lipschitz widths, we want to state and prove a lemma which
shows the behavior of the entropy numbers of an image of a γ-Lipschitz mapping. More precisely,
the following holds.
Lemma 3.1. Consider the two normed spaces (X0 , k · kX0 ) and (X1 , k · kX1 ) and the γ-Lipschitz
map
                 Φ : (K0 , k · kX0 ) → (K1 , k · kX1 ), K0 ⊂ X0 , K1 ⊂ X1 .
Then the following holds:
    (i) if Φ(K0 ) = K1 , then
                                    ε̃k (K1 )X1 ≤ γ ε̃k (K0 )X0 ,    k = 1, 2, . . . .                       (3.1)
       In particular, if Φ : (BYn , k · kYn ) → (BZm , k · kZm ) is a γ-Lipschitz map from the unit ball
       BYn onto the unit ball BZm , then n ≥ m.
 (ii) if Φ(K0 ) approximates K1 with accuracy ε2 and A ⊂ K0 approximates K0 with accuracy ε1 ,
      then Φ(A) approximates K1 with accuracy γε1 + ε2 .
                                                             k
Proof: We ﬁrst prove (i). We consider the set {gj }2j=1 ⊂ K0 of 2k elements of K0 , k ≥ 1, that are
the centers of 2k balls of radius ε ≥ ǫ̃k (K0 )X0 that cover K0 . Let
                                       fj := Φ(gj ),     j = 1, . . . , 2k ,
be the images of these gj ’s under Φ. Then, since Φ(K0 ) = K1 , for every f ∈ K1 there is g ∈ K0
such that Φ(g) = f , and index j ∗ ∈ {1, . . . , 2k } such that kg − gj ∗ kX0 ≤ ε. Therefore we have
                        kf − fj ∗ kX1 = kΦ(g) − Φ(gj ∗ )kX1 ≤ γkg − gj ∗ kX0 ≤ γε,
                          k
which shows that {fj }2j=1 provides a covering for K1 with radius ≤ γε, and thus
                                              ε̃k (K1 )X1 ≤ γε.
The latter inequality is true for any ε being the radius of a set of 2k balls that cover K0 , and
therefore (3.1) holds by taking the inﬁmum over all such ε.
   In the case when K0 = BYn and K1 = BZm , we derive from (3.1) and (2.15) that
                                εk (BYn ) ≥ (2γ)−1 εk (BZm ),       k = 1, 2, . . . .
We know from (1.1.10) in [4] that for any unit ball BXℓ of any Banach space (Xℓ , k·kXℓ ) of dimension
ℓ we have 4 · 2−k/ℓ ≥ εk (B) ≥ 2−k/ℓ , k = 1, 2, . . . . Thus we get
                 4 · 2−k/n ≥ εk (BYn ) ≥ (2γ)−1 εk (BZm ) ≥ (2γ)−1 2−k/m ,               k = 1, 2, . . . ,
which can hold only when n ≥ m.
   To show (ii), we take f ∈ K1 , the corresponding g ∈ K0 such that kΦ(g) − f kX1 ≤ ε2 and g0 ∈ A
such that kg0 − gkX0 ≤ ε1 . So, we have
                    kΦ(g0 ) − f kX1 ≤ kΦ(g0 ) − Φ(g)kX1 + kΦ(g) − f kX1 ≤ γε1 + ε2 ,
and the proof is completed.
                                                                                                                ✷

                                                       11
3.2   A single norm defines the Lipschitz width
In this section, see Theorem 3.3, we extend Lemma 2.1, (ii) and prove that in the deﬁnition of
Lipschitz width the inﬁmum over all norms is achieved for some norm that satisﬁes (2.7). We use
the following version of Ascoli’s theorem, whose proof can be found in [5], and which we state
below.

Lemma 3.2. Let (X, d) be a separable metric space and (Y, ρ) be a metric space for which every
closed ball is compact. Let Fj : X → Y be a sequence of γ-Lipschitz maps for which there exists
a ∈ X and b ∈ Y such that Fj (a) = b for j = 1, 2, . . . . Then, there exists a subsequence Fjk , k ≥ 1,
which is point-wise convergent to a function F : X → Y and F is γ-Lipschitz. If (X, d) is also
compact, then the convergence is uniform.

   Now we are ready to state and prove the following fact.

Theorem 3.3. For any n ∈ N, any compact set K ⊂ X, and any constant γ > 0 there is a norm
k · kY on Rn satisfying (2.7) such that

                                           dγn (K)X = dγn (K, Y )X .

Proof: It follows from Lemma 2.1, (i), (ii) that we can ﬁnd a sequence (Ψj )∞j=1 of γ-Lipschitz maps
Ψj : (BYj , k · kYj ) → X, where the norms k.kYj on Rn satisfy (2.7), such that

                       dj := sup inf kf − Ψj (y)kX → dγn (K)                as   j → ∞.
                              f ∈K y∈BYj

There is a subsequence k.kYjk of the sequence of norms k.kYj that converges point-wise on Rn and
uniformly on Bℓn∞ to a norm k.kY on Rn satisfying (2.7). Indeed, one can check that the functions
Fj : (Rn , k · kℓn1 ) → R, deﬁned as Fj (y) := kykYj satisfy Fj (0) = 0, and

                   |Fj (y ′ ) − Fj (y)| = |ky ′ kYj − kykYj | ≤ ky ′ − ykYj ≤ ky ′ − ykℓn1 ,

where we have used (2.7). Thus, the sequence (Fj )∞     j=1 satisﬁes the conditions of Lemma 3.2 with
γ = 1, a = b = 0, and so we can ﬁnd a subsequence Fjk that converges point-wise on Rn and
uniformly on Bℓn∞ . In fact, the limit function F of this subsequence is a norm, which we denote by
k · kY . Clearly, this norm satisﬁes inequalities (2.7).
     Now, passing to a subsequence, we will assume that k.kYj converge uniformly on Bℓn∞ to the
function k.kY . Thus, there is j0 ∈ N such that for any j ≥ j0 there is εj with the properties
0 < εj < 1 , limj→∞ εj = 0 and

                       kykYj − εj ≤ kykY ≤ kykYj + εj ,           for all    kykℓn∞ ≤ 1.

4     Lipschitz widths and entropy numbers
In this section we discuss the relation between the Lipschitz widths dγn (K)X and the entropy numbers
εn (K)X of a compact set K.

4.1     Lipschitz widths are smaller than entropy numbers
We start with the construction of a particular Lipschitz function that can be viewed as a sum of
‘bumps’, each one supported on a closed ball from a Banach space Y . We use this function to show
that the Lipschitz widths of a compact set K ⊂ X are smaller than the entropy numbers of that
set.

Lemma 4.1. Let (B j ) := (B(yj , ρj )) be a family of disjoint open balls in a Banach space Y . Then
the following holds:
    (i) for every sequence (ϕj ) of γj -Lipschitz mappings ϕj : Y → X, j = 1, 2, . . ., with the property
that ϕj ≡ 0 on the complement of B j , the mapping Φ : Y → X, defined as
                                                    X
                                               Φ0 =     ϕj                                          (4.1)
                                                           j

is a Lipschitz map with Lipschitz constant supj γj .
    (ii) for any sequence (fj ) of elements fj ∈ X with kfj kX = 1 and any sequence (σj ) of real
numbers, the mappings φj : Y → X, j = 1, 2, . . ., defined as
                                          
                                 kyj − ykY
               φj (y) = σj 1 −                 · fj , where (t)+ := max{0, t}, t ∈ R,
                                     ρj      +

are |σj |/ρj -Lipschitz mappings. Their sum, the mapping
                                                 X
                                            Φ :=    φj
                                                           j

is a Lipschitz mapping with Lipschitz constant sup |σj |/ρj and Φ(yj ) = σj fj , j = 1, 2, . . ..
                                                       j

    Proof: To show (i), we denote by γ := supj γj and consider several cases:

    • if y, y ′ ∈ B j , then

                    kΦ0 (y) − Φ0 (y ′ )kX = kϕj (y) − ϕj (y ′ )kX ≤ γj ky − y ′ kY ≤ γky − y ′ kY .

    • if both y, y ′ are outside each of the balls B j , we have kΦ0 (y) − Φ0 (y ′ )kX = 0.
                                               S
    • if y ∈ B j and y ′ is outside the union k B k , we denote by y0 the intersection of ∂B j and the
      line segment connecting y with y ′ . In this case y0 = sy + (1 − s)y ′ for some s ∈ [0, 1]. Then,
      we have Φ0 (y ′ ) = Φ0 (y0 ) = 0 = ϕj (y0 ), Φ0 (y) = ϕj (y), and

       kΦ0 (y) − Φ0 (y ′ )kX = kϕj (y) − ϕj (y0 )kX ≤ γj ky − y0 kY = γj (1 − s)ky − y ′ kY ≤ γky − y ′ kY .



                                                      14
   • if y ∈ B j and y ′ ∈ B k , j 6= k, we denote by y0 the intersection of ∂B j and the line segment
     connecting y with y ′ , and by y1 the intersection of ∂B k and the line segment connecting y
     with y ′ . Then, we have

                                       y0 = s0 y + (1 − s0 )y1 ,   s0 ∈ [0, 1],
                                                               ′
                                       y1 = s1 y + (1 − s1 )y ,    s1 ∈ [0, 1],

      Moreover, Φ0 (y) = ϕj (y), Φ0 (y ′ ) = ϕk (y ′ ), ϕj (y0 ) = 0 = ϕk (y1 ), and therefore

         kΦ0 (y) − Φ0 (y ′ )kX    = kϕj (y) − ϕk (y ′ )kX ≤ kϕj (y) − ϕj (y0 )kX + kϕk (y1 ) − ϕk (y ′ )kX

      For each pair y, y0 and y1 , y ′ we apply the previous case and get

       kΦ0 (y) − Φ0 (y ′ )kX     ≤ γ(ky − y0 kY + ky1 − y ′ kY ) = γ((1 − s0 )ky − y1 kY + s1 ky − y ′ kY )
                                 = γ((1 − s0 )(1 − s1 )ky − y ′ kY + s1 ky − y ′ kY )
                                 ≤ γ((1 − s1 )ky − y ′ kY + s1 ky − y ′ kY )) = γky − y ′ kY .

Since we have considered all possibilities for y, y ′ , we conclude that Φ0 is γ-Lipschitz.
   We now move to proving (ii). It follows from the deﬁnition of φj that it is a function supported
on B j and that Φ(yj ) = φ(yj ) = σj fj . Next, we show that φj is Lipschitz. Indeed, for y, y ′ ∈ B̄ j ,
we have
                                                                     |σj |          |σj |
             kφj (y) − φj (y ′ )kX = kyj − ykY − kyj − y ′ kY              kfj kX ≤       ky − y ′ kY ,        (4.2)
                                                                      ρj             ρj

where we have used that kfj kX = 1. Clearly, if y, y ′ belong to the complement of B j , we have
kφj (y) − φj (y ′ )kX = 0. The third case is when y ∈ B j and y ′ is in its complement. Let y0 be such
that y0 = sy + (1 − s)y ′ for some s ∈ [0, 1] and ky0 − yj kY = ρj , that is, y0 is the intersection of
∂B j and the line segment connecting y with y ′ . In this case φj (y ′ ) = φj (y0 ) = 0, and we can use

                                                   |σj |              |σj |                      |σj |

                                                    ρj                 ρj                         ρj

Thus, φj is a Lipschitz function on Y with Lipschitz constant |σj |/ρj . The fact that the sum Φ is a
Lipschitz mapping with the advertised Lipschitz constant follows from (i) with ϕj = φj . The proof
is completed.                                                                                      ✷

4.2    Estimates for Lipschitz widths from below
We start this section with a lower bound on the Lipschitz constant γ in dγn (K)X . The following

                                                   1 1/n

                                                3
Proof: If dγn (K) < ε, then there is a γ-Lipschitz map Φ and a norm k · kYn , Φ : (BYn , k · kYn ) → X

Lemma 4.5. Let K ⊂ X be a compact set and γ > 0 be a fixed constant. If there is n > n0 ,
n0 = n0 (c0 , α, β) such that

    Lemma 4.5 is similar to the classical Carl’s inequalities [3], traditionally used to provide lower
bounds. However, there is an important diﬀerence. Note that Lemma 4.5 works for each n sepa-
rately, whenever the Carl’s inequality requires an assumption for all j ≤ n. On the other hand the
Carl’s inequality gives the upper bound for εn not εm .
    Next, we continue with a series of results presenting lower bounds for the Lipschitz widths of

with a natural consequence of Proposition 4.4.

4.3   Summary
Now we are ready to state a corollary to Theorem 4.2 and Theorem 4.7.
Corollary 4.8. Let K ⊂ X be a compact subset of a Banach space X, n ∈ N, and dγn (K)X be the
Lipschitz width for K with Lipschitz constant γ ≥ 2 rad(K). Then the following holds:
  (i) For α > 0, β ∈ R, we have
                         [log2 n]β                              γ           [log2 n]β

                     n                                                  n [log2 n]α

(iii) For 0 < α < 1, we have

4.3.1   Lipschitz widths could be smaller than entropy
In this section, we show that the estimates in Corollary 4.8 are sharp and cannot be improved.

4.3.2   The logarithm in Corollary 4.8, part (i) cannot be removed
Here, we provide an example of a compact set K for which the the entropy numbers behave like
n−1 , while the Lipschitz width behaves as [n log2 (n + 1)]−1 .
   We consider the Banach space X = c0 of all sequences that converge to 0, equipped with the
ℓ∞ norm and its compact subset

                                      K(σ) := {σj ej }∞
                                                      j=1 ∪ {0} ⊂ c0 ,                                  (4.26)

determined by the strictly decreasing converging to 0 sequence σ := (σj )∞                ∞
                                                                         j=1 , where (ej )j=1 are the
standard basis in c0 . Since

                                kσj ej − σj ′ ej ′ kℓ∞ = σj ,    for all      j ′ > j,

it follows that the ball with center σj ej and radius σj contains all points σj ′ ej ′ with j ′ > j and
none with j ′ < j. Thus, if we look for 2n balls with centers in K(σ) covering K(σ) with smallest
radius, we take the balls B(σj ej , σ2n ), j = 1, 2, . . . , 2n , with centers σj ej and radius σ2n . Each of
the ﬁrst 2n − 1 balls contain only one point from K(σ), while the last ball B(σ2n e2n , σ2n ) contains
the rest of the points {σj ej }∞
                               j=2n ∪ {0}, which gives

                                              ε̃n (K(σ))X = σ2n .                                       (4.27)

   We next investigate the behavior of dγn (K(σ))X . We shall use the following lemma which gives
upper bounds for the Lipschitz widths for the sets K(σ).

      σjn    =         j         +             j         < n0 +        x         dx = n0 +                         ≤ n0 +          ≤

j=1              j=1                 j=n0 +1                      n0

for γ > 2 and n ≥ n1 (γ, c) ≥ n0 + 1, and σ1 = 1 < γ/2. It follows from Lemma 4.9 that

                                     dγn (K(σ)) ≤ σN = N −c ,                for all    n ≥ n1 ,   N ≥ n0 .

Letting N → ∞ gives that dγn (K) = 0, provided n ≥ n1 . Finally, it is easy to show that the inner
entropy numbers ε̃n (K(σ)) ≍ 2−cn , and the proof is completed.                                 ✷


5           Comparison between Lipschitz and Kolmogorov widths
If we ﬁx the value of n ≥ 0, the Kolmogorov n-width of K is deﬁned as

                  d0 (K)X = sup kf kX ,                   dn (K)X :=              inf    sup dist(f, Xn )X ,        n ≥ 1.           (5.1)
                                      f ∈K                                  dim(Xn )=n f ∈K

It tells us the optimal performance possible for the approximation of the model class K using linear
spaces of dimension n. However, it does not tell us how to select a (near) optimal space Y of
dimension n for this purpose. Let us note that in the deﬁnition of Kolmogorov width, we are not
requiring that the mapping which sends f ∈ K into an approximation to f is a linear map. There
is a concept of linear width which requires the linearity of the approximation map. Namely, given
n ≥ 0 and a model class K ⊂ X, its linear width dL  n (K)X is deﬁned as

                       dL
                        0 (K)X = sup kf kX ,                dL
                                                             n (K)X := inf sup kf − L(f )kX ,                      n ≥ 1,            (5.2)
                                        f ∈K                                     L∈Ln f ∈K

where the inﬁmum is taken over the class Ln of all continuous linear maps from X into itself with
rank at most n.
   We prove in the next theorem the intuitive fact that the Lipschitz width is smaller than the
Kolmogorov width.

                                                                            27
Theorem 5.1. For every compact set K ⊂ X and every n ≥ 1, we have

                    dγn (K)X ≤ dn (K)X ≤ dL
                                          n (K)X ,        for   γ = dn (K)X + rad(K).      (5.3)

Proof: It is clear that dn (K)X ≤ dL n (K)X for every n ≥ 0 since we can take Xn to be the n-
dimensional linear space containing L(X) when L ∈ Ln , so we concentrate on the ﬁrst inequality.
We start with γ > dn (K)X + rad(K), denote

                                      η := γ − dn (K)X − rad(K) > 0,

and choose η1 to be such that 0 < η1 < η. Let Xn ⊂ X be an n-dimensional linear subspace in X
such that,
                               sup inf kf − gkX < dn (K)X + η1 .
                                    f ∈K g∈Xn

For every f ∈ K, we denote by g = g(f ) the element in Xn for which

                                       kf − g(f )kX < dn (K)X + η1 ,                       (5.4)

and the collection of all such elements are denoted by

                                        A = {g(f ) : f ∈ K} ⊂ Xn .

Let us ﬁx g0 ∈ X such that supf ∈K kf − g0 kX < rad K + η − η1 . Then, for every f ∈ K,

                kg(f ) − g0 kX ≤ kg(f ) − f kX + kf − g0 kX < dn (K)X + rad(K) + η = γ,

and therefore

                   rad(A) < γ,      and A ⊂ B(g0 , γ) := {g ∈ Xn : kg − g0 kX ≤ γ}.

We now deﬁne the mapping Φ : (BXn , k · kX ) → X from the unit ball BXn := kg ∈ Xn : kgkX ≤ 1}
in Xn as Φ(g) = g0 + γg. Clearly Φ is a γ-Lipschitz map. Moreover, since Φ(BXn ) = B(g0 , γ) and
A ⊂ B(g0 , γ), we have that

                      sup inf kf − Φ(g)kX ≤ sup inf kf − gk < dn (K)X + η1 ,
                      f ∈K g∈BXn                   f ∈K g∈A

where we have used (5.4) in the last inequality. Thus, using Lemma 2.1, (iii), we obtain

                                          dγn (K)X ≤ dn (K)X + η1 ,

and letting η1 → 0 gives

                         dγn (K)X ≤ dn (K)X ,     for any γ > dn (K)X + rad(K).

Now (5.3) follows from Theorem 2.5 by taking γ → dn (K)X + rad(K).                            ✷

Corollary 5.2. For every n ≥ 1 and every compact set K ⊂ X we have

                                   dγn (K)X ≤ dn (K)X ,   γ = 2 sup kf kX .                (5.5)
                                                                f ∈K


                                                     28
Proof: The inequality follows from Theorem 5.1, Lemma 2.1, (iv), and the fact that for every
n≥1
                               dn (K)X + rad(K) ≤ 2 sup kf kX .
                                                              f ∈K
                                                                                                            ✷
   As a result of this section, we can give the following improvement of Corollary 4.3.

Corollary 5.3. If K ⊂ X is compact, then for every n0 ∈ N ∪ {0} and every γ ≥ dn0 (K)X + rad(K)
we have
                                       lim dγn (K)X = 0.
                                            n→∞

Proof: The statement follows from Theorem 5.1, Lemma 2.1 (iv) and the fact that the sequence
of Kolmogorov widths (dn (K)X ) of a compact set K is a non-increasing sequence of non-negative
numbers that tends to zero, see e.g.[13, Prop 1.2].                                          ✷

5.1   Examples of different behavior of the Lipschitz and Kolmogorov widths
It is intuitively clear that the Lipschitz widths could be much smaller than the Kolmogorov widths.
We illustrate this observation by discussing the following two examples.

Example 5.1. This example, borrowed from Albert Cohen, arises in some partial diﬀerential
equations. We denote by χa the characteristic function of [a, a + 1], a ∈ [0, 1] and consider the
univariate linear transport equation

                                            ∂t ua + a∂x ua = 0,                                          (5.6)

with constant velocity a ∈ [0, 1] and initial condition

                                        u0 (x) = ua (x, 0) = χ0 (x).                                     (5.7)

We denote by
                            H := {χa : a ∈ [0, 1]} ≡ {ua (x, 1) : a ∈ [0, 1]}
the solution manifold to (5.6)-(5.7) evaluated at time t = 1. We prove the following lemma for the
set H.

Lemma 5.4. The Kolmogorov width of H ⊂ L1 [0, 2] is

                                   (n + 1)−1 ≤ dn (H)L1 [0,2] ≤ 4n−1 ,                                   (5.8)

while its inner entropy numbers
                                            ε̃n (H)L1 = 2−n+1 .                                          (5.9)

Proof: We ﬁrst observe that kχa − χb kL1 [0,2] = 2|a − b|. If we deﬁne

                              tj := (2j + 1)2−n−1 ,      j = 0, 1, . . . , 2n − 1,

to be the centers of the intervals [j2−n , (j + 1)2−n ]⊂ [0, 1], we have

            χa ∈ B(χtj , 2−n+1 )    ⇔     kχa − χtj kL1 [0,2] ≤ 2−n+1        ⇔       |a − tj | ≤ 2−n ,

                                                    29
where B(χtj , 2−n+1 ) is the closed ball in L1 [0, 2] with center χtj and radius 2−n+1 . So, those balls
cover H. This calculation also shows that if we have 2n balls covering H and one of them has radius
< 2−n+1 then some other one must have a radius > 2−n+1 . This proves (5.9).
   To show (5.8), we ﬁrst observe that the n-dimensional space
                                     Vn := span{χ̄j ,         j = 0, . . . , n − 1},
where χ̄j is the characteristic function of the interval [2j/n, 2(j + 1)/n] provides an error at most
4n−1 for the elements from H. Indeed, for each χa ∈ H, we have
                                                   j2
                                                   X
                                         kχa −            χ̄j kL1 [0,2] ≤ 4n−1 ,
                                                   j=j1

where j1 = j1 (a) and j2 = j2 (a) are deﬁned as
   j1 (a) = max{j : 2j/n ≤ a, 0 ≤ j ≤ n − 1},                 j2 (a) = max{j : 2j/n ≤ a + 1, 0 ≤ j ≤ n − 1},
and therefore dn (H)L1 [0,2] ≤ 4n−1 . To prove the lower bound in (5.8), we use a well known result,
see e.g. [13, Chap. II, Prop 1.3 ], which states that for any unit ball U in a Banach space X and
any ﬁnite dimensional space Vn+1 of dimension n + 1, the Kolmogorov width
                                               dn (U ∩ Vn+1 )X = 1.                                                  (5.10)
We apply this result for the Banach space X = L1 [0, 2], the unit ball U in L1 [0, 2], and the linear

              Vn+1 = span{ϕ0 , . . . , ϕn },       ϕj := χj/(n+1) − χ(j+1)/(n+1) ,               j = 0, . . . , n.

Therefore

   It follows then from Lemma 5.4 and Theorem 4.2 that the Lipschitz width of H decays expo-
nentially, while its Kolmogorov width decays like n−1 . While this is a good example, one may argue
that this diﬀerent behavior is due to the fact that H is not convex. It is a well known fact that for
every compact set K we have

                        dn (K)X = dn (Kc )X ,       where Kc = conv(K ∪ (−K))

is the minimal convex centrally symmetric set that contains K. Therefore, a more suitable example
would be one when K is a convex, centrally symmetric set. We discuss such case in Example 5.2.

6    Comparison between Lipschitz and stable manifold widths
Let us recall the deﬁnition of manifold width δn (K)X for the compact set K ⊂ X, see [7, 8],

                                 δn (K)X := inf sup kf − M (a(f ))kX ,                          (6.1)
                                                a,M f ∈K


where the inﬁmum is taken over all mappings a : K → Rn and M : Rn → X with a continuous on
K and M continuous on Rn . A comparison between manifold widths and other types of nonlinear
                                                                                      ∗ (K)
widths was given in [8]. There is also another concept, called stable manifold width δn,γ  X of
the compact set K ⊂ X, see [5], deﬁned as
                               ∗
                              δn,γ (K)X :=        inf     sup kf − M (a(f ))kX ,                (6.2)
                                              a,M,k·kYn f ∈K


where now the inﬁmum is taken over all maps a : K → (Rn , k · kYn ), M : (Rn , k · kYn ) → X, and
norms k · kYn on Rn , with a, M being γ-Lipschitz. We discuss in this section the relation between
stable manifold widths and the Lipschitz widths. The next theorem shows that for any compact
set K ⊂ X, the Lipschitz widths are smaller than the stable manifold widths.


                                                         32
Theorem 6.1. For every compact set K ⊂ X, every n ≥ 1, and every γ > 0, we have
                                           2              ∗
                                      dnγ diam(K) (K)X ≤ δn,γ (K)X .                                (6.3)
Proof: We choose ǫ > 0, and let a : K → (Rn , k · kYn ) and M : (Rn , k · kYn ) → X be two γ-Lipschitz
mappings with respect to a norm k · kYn in Rn such that for every f ∈ K,
                                                       ∗
                                   kf − M ◦ a(f )kX ≤ δn,γ (K)X + ǫ.                                (6.4)
For every f1 , f2 ∈ K we have
                                   ka(f1 ) − a(f2 )kYn ≤ γkf1 − f2 kX ,
which implies
                            diam(A) ≤ γ diam(K),           where A := a(K).
We ﬁx an element f0 ∈ K and deﬁne the mapping Φ : (BYn , k · kYn ) → X as
                           Φ(y) := M (a(f0 ) + γ diam(K)y),           a(f0 ) ∈ Rn .
Note that Φ is a γ 2 diam(K)-Lipschitz mapping. For each f ∈ K we deﬁne
                                                1
                                y(f ) :=             (a(f ) − a(f0 )) ∈ BYn .
                                           γ diam(K)
An easy calculation shows that Φ(y(f )) = M ◦ a(f ), so
                                                              ∗
                        kf − Φ(y(f ))kX = kf − M ◦ a(f )kX ≤ δn,γ (K)X + ǫ,
where we have used (6.4). Therefore we obtain
                                 ∗                                2                 ∗
          sup inf kf − Φ(y)kX ≤ δn,γ (K)X + ǫ              ⇒    dγn diam(K) (K)X ≤ δn,γ (K)X + ǫ.
          f ∈K y∈BYn

Since ǫ is arbitrary, (6.3) holds and the proof is completed.                                          ✷
Theorem 6.2. For every Banach space X and for every n ∈ N there exist compact sets K ⊂ X
such that for every γ > 0,

of X. By the Borsuk theorem, see [2, 12], we have that for any continuous map a : K → Rn ,
there exists f0 ∈ K such that a(f0 ) = a(−f0 ), and thus for any map M : Rn → X we have
M (a(f0 )) = M (a(−f0 )). Then, since kf0 kX = 1 and f0 , −f0 ∈ K, we have the inequality
          2 = kf0 − (−f0 )kX = kf0 − M (a(f0 )) + (M (a(−f0 )) − (−f0 )kX                           (6.5)

                                                      33
7     Relation to neural networks
In this section, we discuss deep neural network approximation (DNNA) by feed-forward ReLU
neural networks (NN) of constant width W ≥ 2 and depth n, whose parameters have absolute
values bounded by 1. We will show that the approximation tools provided by these NNs are in fact
Lipschitz mappings
                 Φ : (Bℓñ∞ , k · kℓñ∞ ) → C(Ω),   Ω = [0, 1]d ,    ñ = Cn,      C = C(W ),

with Lipschitz constant γn = C ′ nW n . Therefore, a theoretical benchmark for the performance of
the DNNA for a class K ⊂ X is given by the Lipschitz width dγñn (K)X . This observation motivates
our investigation of Lipschitz widths whose Lipschitz constant depends on n.

7.1   Deep neural networks as Lipschitz mappings
Let us ﬁrst recall that a DNNA of a function f ∈ C(Ω), Ω ⊂ Rd , via feed-forward NN with
activation function σ : R → R, constant width W and depth n is in fact an approximation to f by
the family of functions

                        Σn := {Φ(y) : y ∈ Rñ , ñ = ñ(W, n) = Cn} ⊂ C(Ω).
For each y ∈ Rñ , Φ(y) ∈ C(Ω) is a continuous function Φ(y) : Ω → R of the form

                                Φ(y) := A(n) ◦ σ̄ ◦ A(n−1) ◦ . . . ◦ σ̄ ◦ A(0) ,                   (7.1)
with A(0) : Rd → RW , A(ℓ) : RW → RW , ℓ = 1, . . . , n − 1, and A(n) : RW → R being aﬃne
mappings, and σ̄ : RW → RW given by

                             σ̄(xj+1 , . . . , xj+W ) = (σ(xj+1 ), . . . , σ(xj+W )).
The argument y of Φ is a vector in Rñ that consists of the entries of the matrices and oﬀset vectors
(biases) of the aﬃne mappings A(ℓ) , ℓ = 0, . . . , n. We order these entries in such a way that the
entries of A(ℓ) appear before those of A(ℓ+1) and the ordering for each A(ℓ) is done in the same way.
Before going further, we need to specify a norm k · kYñ to be used for Rñ . We take this norm to be
the ℓñ∞ := ℓ∞ (Rñ ) norm, that is, kykℓñ∞ := max1≤i≤ñ |yi |. This choice is not optimal for obtaining
the best constants in our estimates but it will simplify the exposition that follows. Also, when
considering vector functions g = (g1 , . . . , gW ) from C(Ω), we use the notation
                                           kgk := max kgi kC(Ω) .
                                                    1≤i≤W

    It was proven in [6] that if B is any ﬁnite ball in ℓ∞ (Rñ ) and σ(t) = ReLU(t) = max{t, 0} = t+ ,
then Φ : B → C(Ω) is a γ-Lipschitz mapping with γ depending only on B, W, n, and d. In fact, Φ
is a γ-Lipschitz map on any bounded set. Here, we will investigate in detail the Lipschitz constant
γ in the case when B is the unit ball (Bℓñ∞ , k · kℓñ∞ ). More precisely, the following theorem holds.
Theorem 7.1. The mapping Φ : (Bℓñ∞ , k · kℓñ∞ ) → C(Ω), with Ω = [0, 1]d ⊂ Rd , defined in (7.1)
with σ = ReLU is a C ′ nW n -Lipschitz mapping, that is
                       kΦ(y) − Φ(y ′ )kC(Ω) ≤ C ′ nW n ky − y ′ kℓñ∞ ,     y, y ′ ∈ Bℓñ∞ ,

where C ′ = C ′ (d) is a constant depending on d.

                                                       34
Proof: Let y and y ′ be the entries of the aﬃne mappings A(j) (·) := Aj (·) + b(j) , j = 0, . . . , n, and
A′(j) (·) := A′j (·) + b′(j) , j = 0, . . . , n, respectively, ordered in a predetermined way. We ﬁx x ∈ Ω
and denote by

                         η (0) (x) := ReLU(A0 x + b(0) ),           η ′(0) (x) := ReLU(A′0 x + b′(0) ),

        η (j) := ReLU(Aj η (j−1) + b(j) ),           η ′(j) := ReLU(A′j η ′(j−1) + b′(j) ),       j = 1, . . . , n − 1,
where Aj , A′j , b(j) , b′(j) , j = 1, . . . , n − 1, are the respective W × W matrices and bias vectors,
associated to y and y ′ , and

                                  η (n) := An η (n−1) + b(n) ,     η ′(n) := A′n η ′(n−1) + b′(n) .

Note that since kykℓñ∞ ≤ 1,

kη ′(0) k ≤ (d + 1)kykℓñ∞ ≤ d + 1,          kη ′(j) k ≤ (W kη ′(j−1) k + 1)kykℓñ∞ ≤ W kη ′(j−1) k + 1,        j = 1, . . . , n.

One can show by induction that for j = 1, . . . , n,
                                                                 j
                                                                 X
                                         kη ′(j) k ≤ W j d +           W k ≤ (d + 2)W j .                                 (7.2)
                                                                 k=0

Note that the above inequality also holds for j = 0. Next, since ReLU is a Lip 1 function, we have
                    ′
     kη (0) (x) − η (0) (x)k ≤ k(A0 − A′0 )xk + kb(0) − b′(0) k ≤ (d + 1)ky − y ′ kℓñ∞ =: C0 ky − y ′ kℓñ∞ ,
                              ′
and therefore kη (0) − η (0) k ≤ C0 ky − y ′ kℓñ∞ . Suppose we have proved that

                                          kη (j−1) − η ′(j−1) k ≤ Cj−1 ky − y ′ kℓñ∞ .

It follows that

   kη (j) (x) − η ′(j) (x)k       ≤    kAj η (j−1) (x) + b(j) − A′j η ′(j−1) (x) − b′(j) k
                                  ≤    kAj (η (j−1) (x) − η ′(j−1) (x))k + k(Aj − A′j )η ′(j−1) (x)k + kb(j) − b′(j) k
                                  ≤    W kykℓñ∞ kη (j−1) − η ′(j−1) k + W ky − y ′ kℓñ∞ kη ′(j−1) k + ky − y ′ kℓñ∞
                                  ≤    (W Cj−1 + (d + 2)W j + 1)ky − y ′ kℓñ∞
                                  =: Cj ky − y ′ kℓñ∞ ,

where we have used the induction hypothesis, the fact that kykℓñ∞ ≤ 1, and the bound (7.2) for
kη ′(j) k. Thus, we have obtained that kη (j) − η ′(j) k ≤ Cj ky − y ′ kℓñ∞ , and therefore the following
recursive relation
                           Cj = W Cj−1 + (d + 2)W j + 1, j = 1, . . . , n,
between the constants Cj , j = 1, . . . , n, where C0 = d + 1. We then obtain
                                                           n−1
                                                           X
                        Cn < (n + 1)(d + 2)W +      n
                                                                 W k < C ′ nW n ,     with C ′ = C ′ (d).
                                                           k=0


                                                                 35
Finally, we write

             kΦ(y) − Φ(y ′ )kC(Ω) = kη (n) − η ′(n) k ≤ Cn ky − y ′ kℓñ∞ < C ′ nW n ky − y ′ kℓñ∞ ,

and the proof is completed.                                                                      ✷
   We next discuss a Carl’s type inequality that is similar to Lemma 4.5, but is for the case when
the Lipschitz constant γ depends on n.

Remark 7.2. If one follows the proof of Lemma 4.5 with the condition that γ is not a constant,
but γ = γn = C ′ nδ λn , where C ′ > 0, δ ∈ R, and λ > 1, one can show that

                       [log2 n]β                                                  [log2 m]β

                          n2α                                                        mα
and C, c are fixed constants, depending only on c0 , β, α, δ, λ and C ′ . Indeed, the proof follows

                      N2ε (K) ≤           = (3C ′ c−1 n

7.2    Lower bound for dγnn (K)X
Now that we know that DNNA is an approximation to a function f by a particular γn -Lipschitz
mapping with γn = C ′ nW n , we can ask the question what are the limits of such approximation.
This question is answered by providing a lower bound for the Lipschitz width dγnn (K)X via the next
theorem which is a modiﬁcation of Theorem 4.7.

Theorem 7.3. For any compact set K ⊂ X we consider the Lipschitz width dγnn (K)X with γn =
C ′ nδ λn , δ ∈ R, λ > 1 and C ′ > 0 being fixed constants. Then the following holds:

  (i) if for some constants c1 > 0, α > 0 and β ∈ R we have

                                                         (log2 n)β
                                         εn (K)X > c1              ,    n = 1, 2, . . . ,
                                                            nα
      then there exists a constant C > 0 such that

                                                         (log2 n)β
                                         dγnn (K)X ≥ C             ,     n = 1, 2, . . . .                        (7.3)
                                                            n2α




                                                           36
 (ii) if for some constants c1 > 0, α > 0 we have

                                       εn (K)X > c1 (log2 n)−α ,        n = 1, 2, . . . ,

      then there exists a constant C > 0 such that

                                       dγnn (K)X ≥ C(log2 n)−α ,        n = 1, 2, . . . .                        (7.4)

Proof: We prove the theorem by contradiction. We ﬁrst concentrate on the proof of (i). If (7.3)

                                                       38
7.3   Summary
In this section we summarize our results for the Lipschitz widths dγnn (K)X and give several examples.
The following corollary holds.
Corollary 7.4. Let K ⊂ X be a compact subset of a Banach space X, n ∈ N, and dγnn (K)X be the
Lipschitz width for K with Lipschitz constant γn = C ′ nδ λn , where δ ∈ R, C ′ > 0 and λ > 2.
  (i) For α > 0, β ∈ R, we have

                                          [log2 n]β                               [log2 n]β
                             εn (K)X ≍                   ⇒        dγnn (K)X ≍               ;     (7.10)
                                             nα                                      n2α

 (ii) For α > 0, we have
                                             1                                        1
                             εn (K)X ≍                   ⇒        dγnn (K)X ≍                 .   (7.11)
                                          [log2   n]α                             [log2 n]α

Proof: We ﬁrst prove (i). Let us assume that

                                                             [log2 n]β
                                          εn (K)X ≤ C                  ,
                                                                nα
holds. After using (4.4) from Theorem 4.2, we obtain

                                      n                           [log2 n]β
                                    dn2 rad(K) (K)X ≤ 2β C                  .                     (7.12)
                                                                     n2α
We now ﬁx n0 such that C ′ nδ λn ≥ 2n rad(K) for all n ≥ n0 (recall that λ > 2). We apply Lemma
2.1, (iv) to derive
                                              n
                               dγnn (K)X ≤ d2n rad(K) (K)X , n ≥ n0 .                      (7.13)
Finally, it follows from (7.12) and (7.13) that

                                                    [log2 n]β
                                 dγnn (K)X ≤ C ′              ,      for all n,
                                                       n2α
provided the constant C ′ is chosen appropriately. The other direction in (7.10) is the statement of
Theorem 7.3, (i). The proof of (ii) is similar and we omit it.                                    ✷
    Corollary 7.4 provides a tool for giving lower bounds on how well a compact set (model class)
K can be approximated by a DNN. So far, one way to give such lower bounds is via VC dimension,
see [6], §5.9, and the references therein, which is restricted to the case when approximation error
is measured in the norm k · kC(Ω) . Note that Corollary 7.4 can be applied in the case of Lp
approximation when p 6= ∞. For example, if Bqs (Lτ (Ω)), Ω = [0, 1]d , is any Besov space that lies
above the Sobolev embedding line for Lp (Ω), then it is proven in [9] that

                                   εn (U (Bqs (Lτ (Ω))))Lp (Ω) ≍ n−s/d ,

where U (Bqs (Lτ (Ω))) is the unit ball of Bqs (Lτ (Ω)). Then, according to Theorem 7.1 and Corollary
7.4, we have

               dist(U (Bqs (Lτ (Ω))), Σn )Lp (Ω) ≥ dγñn (U (Bqs (Lτ (Ω))))Lp (Ω) ≥ Cn−2s/d .

                                                        39
In particular, we recover the estimate, see (5.18) in [6]

                              dist(U (Bqs (L∞ (Ω))), Σn )C(Ω) ≥ Cn−2s/d .

Note that, in contrast to stable manifold widths, the Lipschitz widths do not shed a light on the
numerical aspect of this approximation, that is, they do not give even a theoretical algorithm of
how to design the approximant.
